candidateRows: The principal alternatives are later myth, sincere mistake, deliberate deception, and an actual resurrection, forming an exhaustive explanatory framework.
This framework organizes the affirmative case by specifying the rival explanations that the subsequent historical arguments are intended to eliminate.
At the start of his opening case, McLatchie defines four competing explanatory categories before examining evidence for early resurrection belief and reported appearances.
Paul's Corinthian correspondence indicates that resurrection proclamation was already shared with Peter, James, and the original apostolic witnesses.
Establishing an early apostolic origin for the resurrection claim is essential to his attempt to exclude the hypothesis of a much later developing myth.
McLatchie uses the early Corinthian tradition, Paul's description of shared preaching, and Corinthian familiarity with Peter to trace the claim to the apostles.
Acts can reliably report the apostles' early resurrection proclamation because its author accompanied Paul and had access to Jerusalem leaders.
The argument supplies a second route to an early apostolic resurrection claim while defending the source's proximity, authorship, and historical credibility.
McLatchie links the Pentecost report to Luke's claimed investigations, contact with James and other Jerusalem elders, travel with Paul, and narrative travel details.
Internal details about the high priest's household support eyewitness authorship of John and therefore strengthen its resurrection testimony.
The move attempts to ground a canonical appearance account in eyewitness testimony, directly supporting the asserted historical quality of the affirmative evidence.
McLatchie connects named and relational details in the passion narrative with the disciple known to the high priest and the Gospel's beloved-disciple attribution.
The reported appearances were prolonged, collective, and multisensory, making ordinary eyewitness error or hallucination an inadequate explanation.
This directly addresses the sincere-mistake alternative in the affirmative framework and is necessary to the claimed inference toward a real resurrection.
Dillahunty's prior contention that eyewitness testimony is notoriously unreliable.
McLatchie concedes that eyewitness reports can fail under certain conditions but argues that the claimed group encounters differ in duration, familiarity, and sensory range.
The apostles' willingness to suffer and die for their resurrection conviction weighs against their knowingly inventing the claim.
The move is the affirmative case's principal argument against conspiracy, one of the limited alternatives in its purportedly exhaustive explanatory framework.
McLatchie cites the reported deaths of Peter and James, James's conversion, and Peter's changed conduct to argue against conscious fabrication.
Taken cumulatively, early apostolic proclamation, varied appearances, and costly witness commitment make an actual resurrection the best explanation.
The move integrates the affirmative's source, hallucination, and conspiracy arguments into its direct conclusion on the debate's resurrection proposition.
McLatchie summarizes why he considers later myth, honest mistake, and deliberate deception inadequate, then endorses Jesus's resurrection as the remaining explanation.
Strong resurrection evidence should satisfy ordinary standards of admissibility, examination, authenticity, and chain of custody rather than rest on hearsay.
This establishes the skeptical benchmark used to judge the Christian reports and explains why indirect testimony is treated as insufficiently strong evidence.
Dillahunty compares historical claims with courtroom practice, emphasizing physical evidence, examinable witnesses, depositions, authenticity, and preserved custody.
The biblical reports are anonymous, altered, unexamined accounts without identifiable witnesses or corroborating physical evidence, so they cannot establish a resurrection.
This is the skeptical side's direct application to the surviving Christian reports and centrally supports the conclusion that they are too indirect to prove the event.
McLatchie's claim that the Gospel and Acts reports can be grounded in substantially reliable eyewitness testimony.
Dillahunty argues that the reports lack oath, questioning, known transmission history, identifiable degrees of hearsay, and physical means of corroboration.
The poor preservation and indirect character of the resurrection evidence is unexpected if a communicative God intended people to believe it rationally.
This argument connects the alleged divine purpose behind the resurrection with the debate's central complaint that the surviving evidence is indirect and difficult to test.
After discussing what an evidentially responsible God could provide, Matt considers alternative explanations for the absence of clear confirmation, including divine indifference or nonexistence.
The surviving resurrection material falls far below the evidential standard appropriate to an extraordinarily important historical claim.
The move directly answers the motion by comparing the available resurrection reports with the corroboration and investigatory support expected for a strong historical case.
Matt stresses the resurrection's claimed importance, compares its support unfavorably with ordinary legal proof, and catalogs the absence of physical or independently investigable corroboration.
Treating anonymous ancient testimonial material as strong evidence would admit comparably weak supernatural and fraudulent claims under the same standard.
The argument supplies a consistency test for the pro side's evidential standard and claims that accepting it would erase safeguards against unreliable supernatural testimony.
Matt contrasts inaccessible ancient testimony with documented, questioned, and cross-examined witnesses, then compares the offered support with other extraordinary or deceptive claims.
The pro case begins by assuming events needing explanation while overlooking legend as an explanation of the resurrection story itself.
This challenges the pro side's hypothesis set at its foundation by disputing whether a resurrection event, rather than merely a developing story, must be explained.
Jonathan's opening framework of candidate explanations for the reported resurrection events.
Matt argues that Jonathan starts too far downstream by treating a person, death, and resurrection report as facts requiring a causal explanation instead of considering story development.
Legend was included among the exhaustive alternatives, and early Pauline and Lukan material connects the resurrection proclamation to the original apostles.
The move defends the completeness of the pro side's explanatory framework and supports the claim that resurrection belief was early rather than a late legendary development.
Matt's claim that Jonathan's explanatory alternatives omitted legend and began by assuming too much.
Jonathan restates four alternatives, identifies legend as the first, and invokes Pauline tradition, apostolic preaching, and Luke's reported access to witnesses and extended encounters.
Documentary testimony can constitute strong evidence when multiple sources mutually corroborate one another and jointly favor the resurrection explanation.
This directly contests the skeptical evidential standard and states the pro side's central method for treating historical documents as a strong cumulative resurrection case.
Matt's contention that physical evidence is strong while the surviving documentary testimony is inherently weak.
Jonathan analogizes documentary analysis to other evidential settings and argues that several converging sources concerning appearances and the empty tomb provide explanatory power and scope.
The anonymity objection is inconclusive, while contextual and literary considerations support identifying Luke and John as connected to eyewitness testimony.
Authorship and access to eyewitnesses bear directly on whether the principal Christian documents are sufficiently attributable and reliable to support the resurrection historically.
Matt's argument that the gospel reports are anonymous, unsourced, and unavailable for meaningful investigation.

Jonathan argues that missing original manuscripts prevent certainty about initial anonymity, proposes that Luke's addressee likely knew the author, and links Johannine writings to an eyewitness claim.
A miracle's low prior probability warrants greater scrutiny but can still be overcome by a sufficiently powerful cumulative documentary case.
The move addresses the central inference from extraordinary claim to evidential insufficiency by explaining how strong likelihood evidence could overcome even an extremely low prior.
Matt's position that resurrection testimony cannot meet the heightened standard required for a miraculous event.

Jonathan distinguishes prior from posterior probability, uses a lottery example to illustrate cumulative confirmation, and suggests that theism and theological context could also raise the resurrection's prior.
Legend and sincere error remain live alternatives because ancient reports alone do not justify assuming the narrated events occurred as described.
The argument restores nonfraudulent natural alternatives to the comparison and challenges the pro case for reasoning within a narrative whose underlying events remain unestablished.
Jonathan's defense that his four-part framework adequately included and answered the legend alternative.

Matt clarifies his use of legend, rejects beginning from the story's assumed occurrence, notes that sincere believers across many rejected movements can be mistaken, and presses consistency across religions.
Paul, Luke, and John do not provide strong resurrection evidence because their relevant claims are indirect, unverifiable, or anonymously transmitted.
This source-by-source critique directly attacks the historical chain on which the affirmative resurrection case depends, especially eyewitness status, attribution, and testable reliability.
Jonathan's claim that Pauline, Lukan, and Johannine materials form a reliable cumulative documentary case.

Matt argues that Paul did not witness Jesus's life or resurrection, Luke's claimed witness access cannot be investigated, companionship adds no verification, and Johannine authorship remains uncertain.
The surviving reports are anonymous, mutually difficult to reconcile, and too inaccessible to investigation to constitute strong evidence for a resurrection.
This move directly states the skeptical case on the motion by challenging the sources' identity, consistency, testability, and capacity to establish the resurrection.
McLatchie's rebuttal that the Gospel material and related historical details jointly provide strong resurrection evidence.

Dillahunty says the rebuttal repeats earlier points, rejects the dismissal of legendary development, explains what supernatural evidence would need to establish, and concludes that the available reports remain inadequate.
Paul cannot supply firsthand testimony to Jesus's crucifixion merely by reporting what other apostles proclaimed.
The exchange tests whether a principal early Christian source supplies direct testimony or only transmits other people's claims, which bears centrally on evidential proximity.
McLatchie's appeal to testimony in Paul, Acts, and the Gospels as support for Jesus's death on the cross.

Dillahunty distinguishes testimony in general from firsthand witnessing, argues that Paul gives no indication that he attended the crucifixion, and denies that reporting apostolic proclamation makes Paul an eyewitness.
Assuming that Luke had access to a large body of living Jerusalem witnesses is circular when the existence of those witnesses depends on the disputed narrative being true.
The argument attacks a key bridge from authorship and travel associations to eyewitness access, preventing disputed narrative claims from validating their own historical foundation.
McLatchie's claim that the author of Luke-Acts traveled with Paul and therefore had ample access to living Jerusalem witnesses.

After McLatchie links Luke-Acts to Paul and Jerusalem, Dillahunty asks how the asserted body of witnesses is independently known and argues that presuming it simply assumes what the debate must establish.
A person's claim can function as evidence when the claimant has an established record of reliability and truthfulness.
This move supplies the epistemic principle underlying McLatchie's reliance on testimony and prepares his broader inference from source reliability to otherwise uncheckable historical reports.
Dillahunty's distinction between an unsupported claim and evidence capable of establishing that the claimed event occurred.
McLatchie disputes a categorical separation between claims and evidence, using an ordinary assertion by a habitually reliable friend to argue that testimonial statements can rationally alter belief.
A claim is not self-validating; independent information about a claimant's reliability would be the evidence, and that information is unavailable for the anonymous Gospel authors.
The response identifies the missing warrant in the pro case and connects anonymity and non-investigability directly to the insufficiency of resurrection testimony.
McLatchie's argument that a trusted and habitually truthful person's assertion itself constitutes a form of evidence.

Dillahunty argues that prior knowledge of a friend's reliability can support an ordinary claim, but no comparable access exists for the Gospel writers, leaving only anecdotes inadequate for concluding that someone rose.
Numerous subtle interconnections and external confirmations cumulatively show that the Gospel and Acts authors were close to the facts and substantially trustworthy.
This is the developed positive foundation for treating the narratives as historically reliable even where their claims cannot be directly cross-checked, making it central to the pro case.
Dillahunty's contention that anonymous, inaccessible personal testimonies cannot reasonably establish that a resurrection occurred.

McLatchie argues that converging chronological details in John and Mark synchronize without apparent design, then places that example within a cumulative case including other coincidences and extrabiblical corroboration.
Agreement on ordinary Passover-era details can arise from shared circulating stories and does not establish either source independence or the truth of a resurrection.

The move directly denies that the offered reliability example bears sufficient inferential weight toward the resurrection, while presenting shared tradition as a nonmiraculous explanation of agreement.
McLatchie's undesigned-coincidence argument that synchronized details in Mark and John support substantial Gospel trustworthiness.

Dillahunty argues that stories could circulate before either text was written, that agreement and disagreement are both expected under literary or oral dependence, and that mundane convergence does not support resurrection.
Apparent variations between Gospel accounts cannot demonstrate independence when both writers may have drawn their versions from a preexisting shared oral tradition.
This supplies a concrete alternative explanation for textual similarities and differences, undercutting the claimed inference from interlocking accounts to independent eyewitness access.
McLatchie's claim that naturally reconcilable variations are evidence of account independence and therefore of historical reliability.
Dillahunty says a shared source need not be a document or another Gospel because multiple authors could produce differing written versions of stories already circulating through oral tradition.
Shared oral tradition does not defeat undesigned coincidences across distinct narrative units and is a less simple explanation than the events actually occurring.
The response defends the independence and reliability machinery of the pro case against the principal natural explanation offered for convergent Gospel details.
Dillahunty's proposal that apparently independent Gospel variations and interconnections derive from shared circulating oral traditions.

McLatchie argues that oral units would not encompass whole Gospel narratives, that interconnections span distinct stories, and that oral derivation could itself preserve an undesigned coincidence rather than refute it.

If the Gospel resurrection material rests on early apostolic eyewitness testimony, competing explanations must account for the reported encounters, with source trustworthiness and martyrdom counting against deliberate fabrication.
The move connects the preceding reliability debate to the central resurrection inference and identifies considerations intended to reduce the plausibility of deliberate deception.
Dillahunty's argument that sincere or generally reliable reporters may still be mistaken and that miracle reports require stronger discrimination.

McLatchie argues that eyewitness-based Gospel traditions would carry the resurrection encounter claims back to the apostles, requiring comparison of myth, honest mistake, and deception while treating trustworthiness and martyrdom as relevant.
McLatchie's reliance on preferred Christian reports supplies no principled epistemic distinction between those reports and rejected supernatural claims from other religions.
The move attacks the comparative reliability standard underlying the historical resurrection case and demands a non-partisan method for distinguishing competing religious testimony.
McLatchie's appeal to Gospel trustworthiness, apostolic testimony, and martyrdom as evidence against deliberate deception.

After McLatchie argues that trustworthy Gospel accounts and apostolic martyrdom weigh against lying, Dillahunty presses the problem of treating favored Christian reports differently from analogous religious testimony.
The debate concerns strong or sufficient evidence, and anonymous biblical accounts may count as evidence without approaching the strength needed to justify resurrection belief.
The move defines the evidential threshold posed by the motion and separates the existence of some evidence from the claim that the evidence is strong enough.
McLatchie's objection that Dillahunty was dismissing the New Testament material as though it were not evidence at all.

During the question period, Dillahunty clarifies that he accepts bad or anecdotal material as evidence in a broad sense while denying that McLatchie's anonymous textual reports meet the agreed strong-evidence standard.
Vivid narrative details do not establish eyewitness accuracy, and the disputed longer ending of Mark undermines treating the published Gospel as uniformly trustworthy testimony.
The move contests the inference from literary vividness to eyewitness memory and offers a concrete textual-transmission problem for the claimed trustworthiness of a principal Gospel source.
The audience question and McLatchie's broader argument that textual features and detailed narratives support Gospel grounding in reliable eyewitness memory.

Asked how Mark's historical present and vivid details fit his hearsay objection, Dillahunty separates sincere reporting from factual accuracy and develops the longer ending of Mark as a test case in selective trust.
Extraordinary testimony should be assessed case by case for witness trustworthiness, deception, honest error, and prior probability rather than rejected solely because of its unusual content.
The move supplies the proposed epistemic method for comparing resurrection testimony with alien-abduction testimony and therefore answers a recurring methodological objection to the pro case.
Dillahunty's charge that McLatchie accepts Christian claimants while rejecting alien-abduction claimants without an evidential basis for the distinction.

McLatchie answers the comparison with alien reports by listing credibility, deception, error, and prior probability as relevant particulars, then argues that interstellar travel has an extremely low prior probability.

A natural alien-visitation hypothesis need not be less probable than a resurrection that violates known natural regularities, especially when no comparable resurrection has been scientifically verified.
The move directly challenges the prior probability assigned to resurrection and ties the motion's strong-evidence threshold to the absence of independently verified events of the same kind.
McLatchie's argument that the vast interstellar distances make an alien-abduction report vanishingly improbable as a comparison case.

Dillahunty denies that alien visitation is necessarily vanishingly improbable, contrasts a physically possible event with a resurrection, and asks how often a person dead and buried for days has verifiably returned to life.
Female discoverers in an empty-tomb narrative do not increase its credibility, because an author could use that feature strategically and the feature remains part of an unverified claim.
The move rebuts a specific evidential pillar offered for the empty tomb by denying that an allegedly embarrassing narrative detail independently supports the event's historicity.
McLatchie's argument that women as the chief discoverers would have harmed credibility in that culture and thus supports the empty-tomb report.

After McLatchie invokes the criterion of embarrassment, Dillahunty calls the inference unsound, compares it to reasoning about how a criminal would behave, and raises the possibility of a deliberate double bluff.
The Gospels and Acts are substantially trustworthy because multiple inductive considerations connect them to credible eyewitness testimony and informed access to resurrection witnesses.
The move consolidates the pro side's foundation for treating early Christian reports as historically credible sources rather than merely late, anonymous, or inaccessible narratives.
Dillahunty's repeated contention that the surviving Christian writings are anonymous hearsay accounts without adequate access to identifiable eyewitness evidence.

In closing, McLatchie summarizes an inductive trustworthiness case, emphasizes the author's companionship with Paul and Jerusalem access, and uses Pauline agreement with Peter, James, and the Twelve to trace the claim early.
Testimonial claims are evidence when their witnesses are credible, and corroborative relationships between Paul and Acts support treating Paul's resurrection reporting as reliable testimony.
The move answers the debate's central dispute over whether textual claims can function as evidence and connects that principle to a proposed credibility basis for the Pauline material.
Dillahunty's recurring distinction between unsupported claims in Christian texts and evidence capable of establishing that the reported events occurred.

McLatchie argues that a claim's evidential force depends on witness credibility, then invokes alleged undesigned coincidences and Paul's relationship to Acts and Corinthian familiarity with Peter's preaching.
Because the resurrection claim reaches the original apostles, eliminating deliberate fabrication and honest mistake would redistribute probability toward Jesus actually rising from the dead.
The move states the core inferential structure of the pro case: early apostolic origin plus comparative elimination of rival explanations is offered as affirmative evidence for resurrection.

Having defended early and credible testimony, McLatchie presents fabrication, sincere error, and real resurrection as competing explanations and argues that evidence against alternatives raises the resurrection hypothesis's probability.

Multisensory, group, and extended encounters undermine honest-mistake explanations, while willingness to die for the testimony weighs against deliberate lying, leaving resurrection as the best explanation.
The move applies the proposed elimination framework to both principal skeptical alternatives and reaches the pro side's ultimate explanatory conclusion about the resurrection evidence.
Skeptical alternatives according to which the disciples' resurrection reports arose through sincere perceptual error, confusion, invention, or deliberate deception.

McLatchie cites physical contact, conversations, meals, group experiences, and a forty-day span against mistake, then invokes martyrdom as nonconclusive evidence against lying and concludes that resurrection best explains the evidence.
Testimonial claims can constitute evidence, and the available accounts are best explained as grounded in a real resurrection.
This move states the pro side's central epistemic defense of testimony and connects that defense directly to the resurrection conclusion.
Matt's distinction between claims and evidence and his dismissal of testimony as adequate resurrection evidence.
Near the end of his closing statement, McLatchie disputes the skeptical treatment of testimony and argues that the accounts require explanation as mistake, deception, or reality.
McLatchie's reasoning is abductive rather than inductive, and a claim cannot establish itself merely by being labeled evidence.
The move challenges both the form of the resurrection inference and the pro side's foundational treatment of testimonial claims as evidence.
McLatchie's accusation that Matt misunderstands induction and his assertion that claims themselves can serve as evidence.
Dillahunty briefly extends his closing remarks to distinguish credibility evidence from the claim supported by it and to characterize inference to the best explanation as abduction.
The witnesses' habitual trustworthiness and instances of messianic convergence make deception less likely and can overcome a low resurrection prior.
The answer supplies an alternative basis for witness sincerity and directly argues that contextual historical and theological evidence can outweigh a low miracle prior.
The question whether evidence besides martyrdom weighs against apostolic lying and whether lying remains likelier than a miracle.
McLatchie appeals first to the sources' asserted habitual truthfulness, then argues that Passover symbolism and Christianity's global emergence increase the resurrection's contextual probability.
Lying remains more probable than an accurately reported miracle, and the same skeptical standard applies to supernatural claims in any historical book.
This move states the skeptical comparative-probability judgment and rebuts the allegation that the Bible is subjected to a uniquely demanding standard.
McLatchie's answer about whether apostolic lying is more probable than a miracle and a viewer's allegation of a special biblical standard.
Dillahunty clarifies that he need not allege actual dishonesty to regard lying as likelier than accurate miracle testimony, then generalizes his standard to other supernatural histories.
Christian belief is evidence-dependent and could be abandoned if the resurrection case weakened or contrary evidence accumulated sufficiently.
The move addresses whether the resurrection position is falsifiable and identifies declining argument strength and cumulative contrary evidence as potential defeaters.
The question whether McLatchie would remain Christian if the resurrection were shown false and what evidence could count against it.

McLatchie says his Christianity depends on public evidence, discusses the difficulty of identifying Jesus' body, and compares worldview revision to abandoning a scientific paradigm after anomalies accumulate.
A sound evidential standard must explain why Christian reports are accepted while comparable reports from other religions are rejected.
The challenge tests the consistency and discriminatory power of the pro side's epistemology rather than merely disputing one isolated historical detail.
McLatchie's claim that his worldview responds rationally to cumulative evidence and that inconsistent results would undermine his confidence.
Dillahunty argues that McLatchie's admitted willingness to reconsider under cross-religious parity returns to an earlier unanswered problem about accepting Christian accounts but dismissing others.
Religious claims should be distinguished by their case-specific evidence, as illustrated by the Quran's late denial of Jesus' well-attested crucifixion.
This is the pro side's direct answer to the charge of inconsistent standards, offering historical proximity and corroboration as discriminating criteria.
Dillahunty's demand for a standard that justifies accepting Christian accounts while rejecting comparable claims from other religions.
McLatchie answers that particulars matter and contrasts first-century evidence for the crucifixion with the Quran's contrary statement written roughly six centuries later.
A claim may be a data point, but it is not sufficient by itself to establish an extraordinary event such as a resurrection or an empty tomb.
The move articulates the con side's core evidentiary standard and applies it directly to resurrection testimony, multiple reports, and the alleged empty tomb.
The challenge that reports of assault or racism expose a problem in Matt's assertion that claims are not evidence.

Dillahunty distinguishes counting a report as information from treating it as sufficient proof, emphasizes background consistency and source credibility, and denies that multiplying claims demonstrates an empty tomb.
The debate concerns whether the resurrection occurred, not whether miracles are intrinsically unlikely, and sufficient evidence would warrant belief without identifying a cause.
The clarification rejects a major characterization of the skeptical case and identifies evidential insufficiency, rather than an a priori ban on miracles, as its basis.
McLatchie's steelman portraying Matt as holding that miracles are always the least probable explanation and can never be historically inferred.

Dillahunty says he did not argue about a miracle's prior improbability or propose an alternative explanation; he would accept the event given sufficient evidence while leaving its mechanism unresolved.
Literary dependence among the Gospels does not defeat undesigned coincidences because subtle interlockings still provide evidence of historicity.
The move defends a significant supporting argument for Gospel reliability against the objection that shared source material explains the apparent correspondences.
The viewer's objection that non-deliberate coincidences are unlikely or unprovable because the Gospel authors copied from one another.
McLatchie concedes synoptic literary dependence but argues that casual cross-account details about Philip, Bethsaida, and the feeding narrative interlock too subtly to look deliberately manufactured.
Appealing to magic or the supernatural has no explanatory power because an unknown cannot be explained by invoking a still greater mystery.
This states the skeptical standard governing whether a supernatural resurrection can function as an explanation rather than merely rename the unresolved mystery.
The questioner's suggestion that rejecting naturalism as limiting should make rejection of magic equally problematic.
During audience questions, Matt rejects the proposed symmetry between naturalism and magic by arguing that explanations must connect unknowns to things already understood.
Resurrection reports must be assessed by the historical credibility, proximity, truthfulness, and eyewitness basis of their sources, criteria he says favor Jesus over Dionysus.
The move identifies the historical criteria by which the Christian resurrection claim is said to differ evidentially from superficially similar ancient religious reports.
The audience challenge that Dionysus also reportedly rose from the dead in religious texts, creating an apparent inconsistency.
Jonathan answers a comparison with Dionysus by denying that the bare presence of an ancient resurrection report is sufficient and applying reliability and eyewitness criteria.
Jesus has more resurrection reports than Dionysus, but comparative abundance does not establish that the evidence is strong enough to justify accepting the claim.
This directly distinguishes being comparatively better attested from meeting the absolute evidentiary threshold needed to warrant belief in a resurrection.
Jonathan's claim that historically credible and eyewitness-linked Christian sources distinguish Jesus from Dionysus.
Matt concedes a comparatively better case for Jesus because there are more reports, while arguing that the debate turns on adequacy rather than relative superiority.

He need not specify in advance what evidence would prove a resurrection; evidence becomes compelling through a demonstrable causal connection, while accepting the New Testament risks lowering standards for rival claims.
The response defends an open but non-prescriptive epistemic standard and presses the central consistency objection against accepting Christian testimony while rejecting competing accounts.
The audience demand that Matt identify historical evidence that would be necessary and sufficient to compel resurrection belief.
Asked what could convince him, Matt says novel claims need not have predetermined proof conditions and insists that presented evidence must bear a demonstrable causal relation to the claim.
Multiple independent lines of evidence cumulatively reduce the plausibility of myth, conspiracy, and hallucination hypotheses and thereby increase support for resurrection.
This supplies the pro side's core cumulative-case inference: evidence need not individually decide the issue if its combined effect shifts probability away from alternatives.
The challenge to distinguish whether religious claimants such as Paul or Joseph Smith were lying, mistaken, or truthful.
Jonathan answers a religious-claimant comparison by returning to his opening cumulative method and arguing that accumulated evidence disconfirms the principal natural alternatives.
The Gospels are not reliable merely because they claim reliability; their accuracy on independently checkable matters provides reason to trust them where direct checking is unavailable.
The move defends the bridge from corroborated Gospel details to trust in uncheckable resurrection-related assertions, a crucial step in the historical case.
The question whether a dogmatic religious book would portray its own witnesses as trustworthy regardless of their actual credibility.
Jonathan rejects self-attestation as his basis for reliability and instead argues from independently verifiable accuracy to defeasible trust in unverified portions of the accounts.

Undesigned coincidences, external corroboration, unexplained allusions, expressive silences, and related categories cumulatively support general Gospel reliability and defeasible trust in particular claims.
This condenses the affirmative's foundation for treating Gospel assertions as credible even when a particular reported fact lacks direct independent confirmation.
The audience question asking how Jonathan knows that the claims used to establish biblical figures' trustworthiness are themselves true.
Jonathan presents several categories of corroborative and interlocking evidence as a cumulative basis for substantial Gospel reliability, subject to contrary evidence.
Despite repeated references to extra-biblical evidence and support, the resurrection case actually presented relies entirely on biblical material.
The objection attacks the claimed independence of the pro side's corroboration and therefore the evidential foundation offered for trusting the Gospel reports.
Jonathan's repeated claim that extra-biblical corroboration contributes to the cumulative reliability case for the Gospel accounts.
Immediately after Jonathan lists cumulative reliability categories, Matt argues that the purported extra-biblical component never appeared as genuinely independent support in the case.
A proposition is not itself evidence; surrounding facts about the claimant's character, setting, and circumstances may instead constitute evidence bearing on that proposition.
This clarifies the skeptical side's core evidentiary objection to treating testimonial assertions as support without separating the claim from independently probative context.
The follow-up contention that, because evidential status is context-dependent, claims can themselves count as evidence in some contexts.
Matt refines his earlier position by separating propositions from contextual information about their production, suggesting that Jonathan may be counting the latter as evidence.
Willingness to preach despite persecution does not validate Christianity because many religions have faced hostility, making the martyrdom-style inference fundamentally flawed.
The move directly rebuts a common sincerity and martyrdom argument used to infer truth from early Christian commitment and exposure to hostile treatment.
The audience argument that disciples would not preach a lie or found a religion that exposed them to Roman hatred and death.
Matt answers the persecution argument by broadening the comparison class beyond Christianity and denying that costly religious commitment establishes the underlying supernatural claim.
